## Abhidhammapiṭaka
## Dhammasaṅgaṇī-mūlaṭīkā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Vīsatigāthāvaṇṇanā

In the explanation of the Dhamma (the Commentary), paying homage to the Teacher, the Blessed One, is performed to inspire faith in the Blessed One because the Dhamma is well-expounded, and to inspire faith in the Dhamma by manifesting the Blessed One's unerring teaching. Because of faith in these two Jewels, the practice of the Dhamma accomplishes great benefit.

Alternatively, the expression of homage to the Triple Gem is to make known one's own faith in the Triple Gem. Making this known is to please the minds of the wise. Pleasing them is to encourage the acceptance and learning of the Commentary. Such learning is to achieve all mundane and supramundane attainments (sampatti).

The specific purpose intended by the Teacher (the Commentator) in this work is the removal of obstacles. He will himself state later: "By the power of this homage, having completely removed obstacles..." Paying homage to the Triple Gem is capable of removing obstacles because it is a special merit that destroys the demerit that causes obstacles, because it is auspicious, and because it wards off dangers and calamities.

How is it known that this homage destroys demerit? It is known from such words as: "Mahānāma, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not overwhelmed by lust" (A. Ni. 6.10); and "Honoring those worthy of honor, this is the highest blessing" (Khuddakapāṭha 5.3); and "Monks, for those who thus recollect the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, no fear, trepidation, or hair-standing-on-end will occur" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.249).

In that [opening of the Commentary], desiring to pay homage to the Blessed One who is the Teacher, he spoke the verse beginning with "Karuṇā viya" to show the special qualities of that Blessed One. For only a person endowed with special qualities is worthy of homage...
2:
...is worthy of homage, and homage paid to one worthy of homage indeed brings about the stated benefits. The teaching of the Blessed One is primarily characterized by compassion in the Vinaya Piṭaka, and primarily by both wisdom and compassion in the Suttanta Piṭaka. For that very reason, when composing the explanation (saṃvaṇṇanā) of the Vinaya Piṭaka, praise of the Blessed One was made with compassion as the primary focus; and when composing the explanation of the Agamas (Suttas), praise was made with both as the primary focus. However, since the Abhidhamma teaching is primarily characterized by wisdom, desiring to make praise with wisdom as the primary focus, he praises [the Buddha] through wisdom, taking compassion as a simile, saying "Karuṇā viya sattesu" (Like compassion towards beings).

In that verse, "Karuṇā viya" is a statement indicating a simile. The meaning is: just as compassion functioned towards all beings for that Blessed One, so too did wisdom function towards all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma). "Sattesu" (towards beings) indicates the object [of compassion]. "Paññā" (wisdom) indicates the thing to be illustrated (the subject of the simile). "Yassa" (for whom) indicates the person who is the locus of those qualities. "Mahesino" (of the Great Seeker) is an epithet for that person. "Ñeyyadhammesu" (towards knowable things) indicates the object of wisdom. "Sabbesu" (towards all) is an epithet for those knowable things. "Pavattittha" (functioned) indicates the action. "Yathāruci" (according to wish) indicates the power of mastery (vasībhāva).

In that context, it is called "Karuṇā" because it dispels (kirati); the meaning is that it removes or clears away the suffering of others. They are called "Satta" (beings) because they are attached (visatta) to objects such as forms. Because that designation (paññatti) of "beings" is firmly established in the continuity of the aggregates, even Arahants who are free from desire and lust are called "beings." It is called "Paññā" (wisdom) because it knows distinctly (pajānāti); the meaning is that it penetrates things according to their true nature in various modes. "Yassa" has an indefinite meaning. The definite reference should be understood by the words "tassa pāde namassitvā" (having bowed at his feet). He is called "Mahesī" because he sought (esi/gavesī) the great (maha) groups of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth. They are called "Ñeyya" because they are to be known. They are called "Dhamma" in the sense of bearing their own nature, etc. Therein, by the word "Ñeyya," he rejects the notion that phenomena are unknowable. By the word "Dhamma," he rejects the notion that knowable things are "beings" or "souls" (jīva), etc. They are "Ñeyyadhamma" because they are both knowable and are phenomena (dhamma). "Sabbesu" (in all) means taking them without exception. By that word, he shows that there is nothing unknown. "Pavattittha" means it arose or occurred. "Yathāruci" means occurring according to whatever wish there may be. "Ruci" (wish) is the desire or the will to act. Wisdom occurred in those various ways according to whatever wish arose. Or, it is said to have "occurred yathāruci" because it occurred in accordance with his wish. Or, wisdom occurred in whatever manner the wish occurred.

In that verse, only the compassion existing in the Blessed One's own mental continuity should be taken as the simile for the Blessed One's wisdom. That is indeed the unique Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā), and no other. The word "Yassa" indicates the person who is the locus of both compassion and wisdom. Indeed, there is no compassion without a locus.
3:
When "compassion" is mentioned, the person who is the locus of that compassion must be pointed out. In this verse, there is no person other than the one indicated by "yassa" (of whom). Since there is no benefit in passing over the person nearby to take one far away, the person indicated by "yassa" is indeed the locus of compassion. Therefore, this means: "In that Blessed One, wisdom functioned just like great compassion."

How did great compassion function among beings, and how did wisdom function among phenomena? It functioned both exhaustively and according to his wish. For the Blessed One's compassion functions towards all beings without exception, leaving no one out. And when it functions, it does so according to his wish, uniquely and specifically for one or many beings, in a way not shared by others (asādhāraṇa). For others, seeing beings plunged into the great flood of the fourfold whirlpool of saṃsāra, do not experience the descent of compassion as the Blessed One does, thinking, "There is no one else but me to pull these beings out of the flood."

The Blessed One's wisdom also functions towards all phenomena without exception. And when it functions, it does so according to his wish, uniquely and specifically for one or many phenomena, knowing their nature, function, etc., without obstruction and in a way not shared by others. Just as the Blessed One's compassion functions according to his wish, so too does his wisdom. All aspects of how compassion functions according to his wish should be understood through the Mahākaruṇāñāṇavibhaṅga in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. How wisdom functions according to his wish should be understood through the remaining Asādhāraṇañāṇavibhaṅga, and so on.

By the term "wisdom," the knowledge unobstructed in the three times, the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths, and the four knowledges of analytical insight (paṭisambhidā) are taken. Since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is already taken by the term "compassion," excluding that, the other five unique knowledges (asādhāraṇañāṇa), the four knowledges of intrepidity (vesārajja), the ten powers (dasabala), the six higher powers (abhiññā), the forty-four bases of knowledge (ñāṇavatthu), the seventy-seven bases of knowledge, and many other varieties of wisdom are included. Therefore, the functioning according to his wish should be understood through the functioning of each of those knowledges. Thus the commentator said, "Like compassion... according to his wish."

In that verse, by the mention of compassion, the root of Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi) is shown. For, seeing the multitude of beings oppressed by great suffering, his mind was urged by compassion, thinking, "There is no other refuge for these beings; having liberated myself, I shall liberate them." Thus, having made the initial resolution (abhinīhāra) at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, and having fulfilled the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), he gradually attained Supreme Enlightenment. Therefore, compassion is the root of Great Enlightenment. By the word "sattesu" (among beings), the purpose of Great Enlightenment is shown. Beings are the reason for Great Enlightenment. For omniscience was aspired to for the sake of delivering beings. As it is said in the Buddhavaṃsa:
4:
"What is the use of me, a man who has seen his own strength, crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra alone? Having reached omniscience, I shall deliver the world together with the devas." (Buddhavaṃsa 2.56).

By the word "wisdom," Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi) is shown. This is because Path Knowledge (maggañāṇa), which is the proximate cause of omniscience, and Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), which has Path Knowledge as its proximate cause, are called "Great Enlightenment." By the phrase "in all knowable things," it shows all phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), truths (sacca), faculties (indriya), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), categorized as wholesome and so on, which are to be known through higher knowledge, full understanding, abandoning, developing, and realizing by the beings to be delivered. By the phrase "functioned according to his wish," it shows the fulfillment of the benefit by illustrating the functioning of teaching knowledge (desanāñāṇa) preceded by penetration (paṭivedha) and reflection (paccavekkhaṇa). For the knowledge of penetration into all phenomena occurred at the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka). Indeed, that is Path Knowledge itself. Reflective knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) also occurred there, and specifically during the week at the Jewel House (Ratanaghara). Thus, teaching knowledge occurred in the preaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta and others, based on the phenomena thus penetrated and reflected upon; and specifically in the preaching of the seven books of Abhidhamma on the Paṇḍukambala stone. When the Blessed One teaches with teaching knowledge, he practices for the welfare of beings. By all this, the practice for one's own benefit (attahita-paṭipatti) and the practice for the benefit of others (parahita-paṭipatti) are shown. By showing Great Enlightenment, the practice for one's own benefit is shown; by the other words, the practice for the benefit of others is shown. By showing this, it is demonstrated that among the four types of persons, such as the one who practices for his own benefit, the Blessed One is the fourth type of person. Because of this, it shows that he is the unsurpassed object of offerings (anuttara-dakkhiṇeyya), worthy of supreme salutation, and that he has become the supreme field (khetta) for one's own act of salutation.

Furthermore, here, by the mention of compassion, because it illustrates the unique quality that has reached the state of the sublime (mahaggata) among mundane things, the Blessed One's fulfillment of all mundane qualities is shown. By the mention of wisdom, because it illustrates the Path Knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship which is the proximate cause of omniscience, the fulfillment of all supramundane qualities is shown. By the word "compassion," his approaching (beings) is shown to be without defilement; by the word "wisdom," his departing (detachment) is shown. In showing his approaching, his being born and raised in the world is shown; in showing his departing, his being unsullied by the world is shown. By the words "like compassion among beings," the Blessed One's functioning in accordance with worldly convention is shown. By the words "in all knowable things, wisdom functioned according to his wish," it shows that he does not overstep convention. For if there is no penetration into the nature of all phenomena, one oversteps convention and wrongly grasps that "a being exists, a soul exists." Among all the Buddha's qualities, compassion is the beginning, because it is their fundamental cause; wisdom is the end.
5:
Furthermore, it is said thus because there is nothing more to be done, and because by showing the beginning and the end, all the qualities of the Buddha have been shown. By taking compassion (karuṇā), the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), which is preceded by the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), is shown. Indeed, virtue has compassion as its root, because it arises from the abstinence from taking life and so forth due to that compassion. That virtue is also associated with the three jhānas. By the word 'wisdom' (paññā), the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) is shown. Virtue is the beginning of all the Buddha's qualities, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end. In this way, all the Buddha's qualities, which are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, have been shown.

Having thus praised the Blessed One briefly with all the Buddha's qualities, and desiring to provide an exposition of that Abhidhamma teaching, he said "dayāya tāya" and so forth to praise it by means of that Abhidhamma teaching which is not shared with others. To show the origin (nidāna) and the cause (samuṭṭhāna) of that teaching, the words "dayāya tāya" etc. were spoken. The origin is of two kinds: internal and external. The internal origin is compassion, and the external origin is the place, time, and so forth. The cause (samuṭṭhāna) is the teaching-wisdom (desanā-paññā). Among those two, desiring to show the internal origin, he said: "dayāya tāya sattesu, samussāhitamānaso" (with a mind impelled by that compassion for beings). In that context, by "dayā", compassion (karuṇā) is intended. Being well-impelled by that compassion, he set forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse. This word "tāya" (by that) is a re-indication (paṭiniddesa) of the meaning previously mentioned.

In the preceding verse, wisdom was indicated as the primary factor, and compassion was indicated as the modifier (visesana) of that wisdom. Since that compassion is the illustration (upāmāna) of that wisdom and is secondary, it recedes after qualifying that wisdom; therefore, is it not the case that it does not deserve to be re-indicated as "tāya"? Wisdom, which is primary, is only the cause of the teaching and is not the factor that impels; therefore, is it not also inappropriate to re-indicate that wisdom? The statement that it is inappropriate to re-indicate wisdom is correct. However, the re-indication of compassion is not inappropriate because the two words "dayāya tāya" are in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa), having the same referent. Two words in apposition exist in the relationship of modifier (visesana) and the modified (visesitabba), like the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so forth. The word 'form' (rūpa) is the modifier because it is spoken to exclude other aggregates, and the word 'aggregate' (khandha) is the modified because it is a general term for both the aggregate to be excluded and the aggregate to be taken. Similarly, here too, the two words "dayāya tāya" which have the same case ending are in the relationship of modifier and modified because they are in apposition. Therein, compassion (dayā) is primary because it is the impelling factor, and it is also a general term for both the ordinary compassion to be excluded and the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) to be taken. Therefore, this word "dayāya" is the modified term, and as for how it is the modifier of that dayā...
6:
This word "tāya" should likewise be construed as its re-indication (paṭiniddesa). This is because the word "tāya" cannot be a modifier of "dayā" when re-indicating wisdom, but it can be so when re-indicating compassion. Setting aside the primary wisdom, this word "tāya" which is connected with the word "dayāya" is fit to be the re-indication of the secondary compassion. The meaning here is: the compassion by which he was impelled is not just any compassion, but it is the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) which is the manifestation of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa); he was impelled by that Great Compassion.

How is it known that compassion is "dayā"? In the commentary on the word "dayāpanno", it is said "one who has attained a mind of loving-kindness (mettā)", therefore it might be argued that dayā should be mettā and not karuṇā. If that were so, in the commentary on the word "adayāpanno", it is said "one who has attained a state of being void of compassion (karuṇā)", so the view that dayā is mettā would also be inappropriate. Therefore, the word dayā should be construed according to the intended meaning wherever it occurs. It is not inappropriate that the word dayā, when occurring with the internal sense of protection, applies to both loving-kindness and compassion. Only if understood this way will there be no contradiction between the commentaries. And compassion is spoken of as the origin (nidāna) of the teaching, not loving-kindness, in such passages as: "Indeed, at that time the Blessed One dwelt entirely in the dwelling of compassion (karuṇā-vihāra)." Therefore, it should be understood that in this context, only compassion is taken by the word dayā. For only that compassion has the nature of impelling, whereas loving-kindness does not have the nature of impelling but occurs according to the tendency of wisdom.

Why is it said "sattesu" (among beings)? Is it not the case that by the word "tāya", compassion having beings as its object is already taken? It is not that it is not taken; it has been taken. However, in the preceding verse, by saying "compassion occurred among beings as desired", both compassion with a limited (sappadesa) object of beings and compassion with an unlimited (nippadesa) object of beings were mentioned. But in this verse, to take the unlimited object of beings, he said "sattesu" to show the state of having an unlimited object of beings. By showing this, it is shown that being impelled by compassion which has all beings as its object, he well-established the path of the Abhidhamma discourse for the devas and brahmas, and not merely for the sake of devas and brahmas as objects. Therefore, the meaning is already shown that he established the path of the Abhidhamma discourse for the devas and brahmas for the benefit of all beings, and not for the benefit of the devas and brahmas alone. Alternatively, this word "sattesu" is not an indication of the object of dayā, but rather the sphere (visaya) of the impelling (samussāhana) is shown by this word. For the sake of establishing the path of the Abhidhamma discourse, compassion [impelled] the Blessed One not only among the devas...
7:
Great compassion urges the Buddha toward all beings who are capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths. This is understood because the sequence of the Abhidhamma teaching proceeds for the benefit of all beings. Therefore, in the phrase 'sattesu samussāhitamānaso' (with a mind urged toward beings), it should be understood as having a mind directed toward beings who are either the objects or the signs [of that compassion].

Having thus shown the internal origin (abbhantara-nidāna), he says 'pāṭihīrāvasānamhi' and so forth to show the external origin (bāhira-nidāna). Therein, the phrase 'pāṭihīrāvasānamhi vasanto' (dwelling at the conclusion of the miracle) is stated to show the time when the Blessed One set forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse. Because of the statement 'avasānamhi vasanto tidasālaye' (dwelling in the abode of the Thirty-three at the conclusion), it should be understood that 'pāṭihīra' here refers to the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree, at the conclusion of which he dwelt in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. It should be understood that it does not refer to the miracles performed at the foot of the Bodhi tree and elsewhere, nor to the miracles of mind-reading (ādesanā) and instruction (anusāsanī). It should be noted that only the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree is taken here because of its fame and proximity.

Regarding the etymology of the word 'pāṭihāriya', some say: 'It is called pāṭihāriya because it removes (harana) opposing states, such as lust and other defilements.' However, for the Blessed One, there are no opposing states like lust to be removed. Even for worldlings (puthujjana), the supernormal power of various forms (iddhividha) occurs only when the mind is free from defilements and endowed with the eight qualities [of the fourth jhāna], having removed opposing states. Therefore, it is not appropriate to use the term 'pāṭihāriya' here based on the usage applied to the supernormal powers of worldlings.

If, however, one considers the defilements in the mental continuities of beings to be led (veneyya) as the 'opposing states' for the Blessed One, who is possessed of great compassion, then it is appropriate to call it 'pāṭihāriya' because it removes them. Alternatively, it is called 'pāṭihāriya' because it removes the heretics (titthiya) who are opponents of the Blessed One and the Dispensation (Sāsana). For those heretics are removed and set aside by supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction, through the removal of their wrong views and their inability to proclaim their views.

Alternatively, the word 'paṭi' signifies the meaning of 'pacchā' (afterwards). Therefore, it is called 'paṭihāriya' because it is performed afterwards by a mind that is concentrated, free from defilements, and has completed its task. Or, it is called 'pāṭihāriya' because it is a power that removes [defilements in others] after one's own defilements have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the Path. The miracles of supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction are performed again for the benefit of beings after one is free from defilements and has completed the task. Because they remove the defilements of others after one's own defilements have been removed, they are called 'paṭihāriya'. 'Paṭihāriya' is the same as 'pāṭihāriya'. Alternatively, each individual power occurring in the collection of supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction is called 'pāṭihāriya'.
8:
In another way, 'paṭihāriya' (miracle) refers to the fourth jhāna and the Path because they remove opposing states. It is called 'pāṭihāriya' because it arises in that fourth jhāna or the Path which removes opposing defilements, or because it has those states as its basis, or because it proceeds from them. Here, 'paṭihāriya' is simply called 'pāṭihīra'. By the words 'dwelling at the conclusion', he indicates the time. For the time of setting forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse is delimited by the conclusion of the performance of the miracle and the dwelling in the abode of the Thirty-three. By the word 'tidasālaya' (abode of the Thirty-three), he indicates the location. Since it was set forth by him while dwelling in that Tāvatiṃsa heaven, that place is the location for the setting forth of the path of the Abhidhamma discourse.

To show the specific location within that Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he said 'at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree' and so forth. 'Yugandhara' is one of the seven mountain ranges, with a height of 42,000 yojanas. The sun usually travels in the sky at a height equal to that mountain. The meaning is that just as the sun shines at the peak of Mount Yugandhara, so the Blessed One sat there shining brilliantly.

## 4-5. Now, wishing to point out the individuals who would receive the Dhamma, he spoke the verse beginning with 'cakkavāḷasahassehi' (from ten thousand world systems). 'Sabbaso' means from all surrounding directions, or from the ten thousand world systems that are situated together. It does not mean ten thousand world systems from each individual direction. If it were so, it would imply coming from forty thousand world systems or more, which is not intended. Alternatively, it should be connected as 'sitting together evenly all around'. 'Sannisinnena' (sitting together) means sitting evenly without obstructing one another, or sitting with respect for the Blessed One, lending an ear, and avoiding the faults of sitting that should be avoided. It should be construed as 'surrounded by the host of devas with the mother at their head', or 'he well-proceeded with the path of the Abhidhamma discourse with the mother at the head'.

Now, wishing to show the origin of the teaching, he said 'tassā paññāya tejasā' (by the power of that wisdom). That wisdom, which was compared to compassion in the opening verse, is capable of knowing the true nature of all knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma), capable of knowing the various ways in which those things should be taught, and capable of manifesting the inclinations (āsaya) and dispositions (adhimutti) of the individuals to be enlightened. The meaning is that he well-proceeded [with the teaching] due to the association of that Omniscient Wisdom with the three aforementioned powers. By this Pali 'tassā paññāya tejasā', he shows that only Omniscient Wisdom is capable of being the origin of the Abhidhamma discourse, and no other wisdom is capable, thus demonstrating the unique (asādhāraṇa) nature of the Abhidhamma discourse. 'Magga' means means (upāya). It is called 'abhidhamma-kathā-magga' (the path of the Abhidhamma discourse) because it is the means for the penetration of the dhammas such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense-bases (āyatana), and wholesome states (kusala) and so forth, or because it is the means for the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Alternatively, a sequence (pabandha) is called 'magga'. Because the Abhidhamma teaching is long and resembles a road, it is called 'abhidhamma-kathā-magga'. Therefore, the sequence of the Abhidhamma teaching is called 'magga'.
9:
It is called "Abhidhammakathāmagga" because it is the means (upāya). Alternatively, a continuity (pabandha) is called "magga." Because this Abhidhamma Dhamma is long, it is like a path; therefore, the continuity of the Abhidhamma discourse is called "Abhidhammakathāmagga." After saying "surrounded by a host of devas," the use of the word "devānaṃ" again indicates their capability to listen to the Dhamma. This is because the Blessed One does not teach those who are incapable of listening.

Thus, having shown the Blessed One's worthiness of supreme prostration through His attributes headed by compassion and wisdom, and through His practice for the welfare of beings by setting forth the continuity of the Abhidhamma discourse, he now says, "having bowed at the feet of that Blessed One," desiring to perform the intended prostration. By praising the Blessed One alone, the well-expounded nature (svākkhātatā) of the Dhamma and the good conduct (suppaṭipannatā) of the Saṅgha are also shown. This is because the Dhamma and Saṅgha, which originate from that Buddha, do not deviate from those attributes. Therefore, desiring to also bow to those two Jewels worthy of prostration, he says, "having honored His sublime Dhamma... and having performed salutation to the Saṅgha." In that prostration, because it is said of the Blessed One, "In the world with its devas, the Tathāgata is worthy of worship," and of the Saṅgha, "Of good conduct... worthy of salutation," it is therefore said, "having bowed at the feet of that Blessed One, and having performed salutation to the Saṅgha." As for the Dhamma, being endowed with attributes such as well-expoundedness, it should be honored by recollecting those attributes. Because of the words, "One should live respecting, revering, and relying on that very Dhamma," it should be honored in every way with body, speech, and mind. Therefore, it is said, "having honored His sublime Dhamma." In the word "sirīmato," some say "sirī" is a synonym for wisdom (paññā) and merit (puñña). Alternatively, the excellence of physical beauty and so on, arising from merit, depends on one who has performed merit, or is depended upon by those who have performed merit; thus it is called "sirī" (glory/fortune). Since that glory exists pre-eminently in the Blessed One, the Blessed One is called "sirīmā." (Connect with: "having bowed at the feet of) that glorious Blessed One."

"Nipaccakārassa" refers to the performance of the act of bowing. "Ānubhāvena" means by the power. "Sosetvā" means having dried up or caused to disappear (the dangers), and it should be connected with "I shall clarify the meaning." "Antarāye" refers to the dangers that obstruct the clarification of the meaning. "Asesato" means entirely, without remainder.

Now, to show the difficulty of clarifying the meaning because the Abhidhamma has a profound meaning, he shows the request with the verse beginning with "visuddhācārasīlena." He is of "pure conduct" (visuddhācāra) due to purity from offenses such as thullaccaya. He is of "pure virtue" (visuddhasīla) due to purity from pārājika and saṅghādisesa offenses.
10:
Alternatively, he is of pure conduct and virtue (visuddhācārasīla) due to the purity of virtue regarding performance (cāritta) and avoidance (vāritta). "Sakkaccaṃ" means respectfully (acting as if with heart, even if not). "Abhiyācito" means being requested face-to-face. By saying so (that he was respectfully requested), he shows that it is impossible to be disrespectful in clarifying the meaning.

Now, to show that Abhidhamma whose meaning he wishes to clarify, he spoke the verse beginning with "yaṃ devadevo." Therein, "yaṃ" refers to the Abhidhamma. "Devadevo" is because He is the God (deva) of the devas by purity (visuddhi), by convention (sammuti), and by rebirth (upapatti). In the world, those who should be approached as a refuge and a resort are called "devas," and the Blessed One is the resort of all devas. "Nayato" means briefly. "Samācikkhi" means He explained well so that the Elder (Sāriputta) could understand. He is called "Vināyaka" because He disciplines veneyya beings (those ready to be disciplined); or it means "Sayambhū" (Self-Enlightened), being without a leader/guide.

10-12. "Yañca" should be connected as "and which Abhidhamma He taught and recited to the monks." "Payirudāဟာsi" means He taught and recited. "Iti" means in this sequence. In "yo dhārito," the accusative case "yaṃ" changes to the nominative "yo" when connected with the nominative "dhārito"; therefore, the construction should be: "I shall clarify the meaning of that Abhidhamma which was upheld and which was rehearsed in council." By that Sage (muni) called "Vedeha" because he strives (īhati) or proceeds by means of knowledge (veda/paññā). "Abhiṇhaso" means many times. The word "abhidhammassa" should be joined with "I shall clarify the meaning." Now, to show the basis (the old commentaries) for clarifying the meaning, he spoke the words beginning with "ādito." Therein, "ādito" means at the beginning, in the First Council.

Which commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) was rehearsed in council? If asked "of which text is that the commentary?", since there is no other subject mentioned, it is understood by the context of the statement "I shall clarify the meaning of which" that it is the commentary of that Abhidhamma. "Saṅgītā" means it was spoken by collecting it at appropriate places to clarify the meaning, saying "this is the meaning of this word, this is the meaning of this word"; and later it was also rehearsed in the Second and Third Councils.

14-16. "Abhisaṅkhatā" means composed. "Tato" means from the commentary. "Tantinayānugaṃ" means following the way of the sacred texts (Pali). "Bhāsaṃ" means the Magadhan language. "Nikāyantaraladdhီhi" means with the views of other sects inserted here and there. "Asammissaṃ" means unmixed. "Anākulaṃ" means undisturbed and well-defined even within one's own sect. Clarifying the decision on the meaning by the dwellers of the Mahāvihāra, which is unmixed with the views of other sects and undisturbed, I shall explain the meaning.
11:
By the word "I shall clarify" (pakāsayissāmīti), the Theravāda spoken by the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga and others is also included. Alternatively, having removed the Sinhalese language and translated it into the Māgadha language, the meaning of the Abhidhamma being shown is unmixed with the views of other sects and is uncomplicated within its own tradition, being the decision of the Mahāvihāravāsins. Clarifying that meaning as "This is the decision of the Mahāvihāravāsins," I shall explain it. By that very explanation, that meaning is thus demonstrated (as the decision of the Mahāvihāravāsins).

Regarding the phrase "pleasing the wise" (tosayanto vicakkhaṇe), some interpret it by connecting it with "having taken what should be taken," saying that it means pleasing them by showing that "taking only what is appropriate to be taken is very good." If that were the case, the pleasing would be achieved only by taking what should be taken, and it would lead to the fault that pleasing cannot be achieved by explaining other meanings. However, if one connects it as "pleasing [them], I shall explain the meaning," then since taking what should be taken and all other explanations of meaning are included, the pleasing is achieved by all of them. Therefore, the connection "pleasing [them], I shall explain the meaning" is more appropriate.

18-20. Now, desiring to explain the meaning, he speaks the words beginning with "kammaṭṭhānāni" to avoid [the difficulty of] the greatness of that meaning. In the word "atthavaṇṇanā," "vaṇṇanā" means speaking by opening up and expanding. "Iti" means in the manner already shown, such as "having removed the language from there," and so on. In this way, he shows the reason for generating enthusiasm in the listeners. "Abhidhammakathā" refers to the Abhidhamma Commentary. "Listen" (nisāmetha) means to hear. Now, wishing to firmly encourage them that this commentary is certainly worth listening to, he says, "For this talk is rare to find."

## The explanation of the twenty verses is finished.

## Explanation of the Introductory Discourse (Nidānakathā)

Teachers who wish to explain the Atthasālinī Commentary should first clarify the structure and divisions of that commentary. Therefore, this is said:

"The meaning of the word 'Abhidhamma', the divisions, the structure of the Pali text,
the reflection upon it together with the oceans, and the profundity through the teachings."
12:
"The body of the teaching, the grasping of its occurrence, and likewise
the state of being practiced in the path of recitation of the Elder.

"Penetration, and likewise the establishment of the state of being an Abhidhammika
of the All-Seeing One, starting from the Buddha's words and so on.

"The fact of its being spoken is demonstrated by the Vinaya, and also by the Gosinga Sutta
spoken by the Great Sage, and by the Nidāna (Introduction).

"Having clarified all this, the promised discourse is made;
this structure and division in the Atthasālinī should be understood."

Considering that the discourse on Abhidhamma would be beautiful when spoken to one who already knows the general meaning of Abhidhamma through knowing the meaning of the word "Abhidhamma," and because it is appropriate to first distinguish and know the Abhidhamma, he asks the question to make that meaning known: "In what sense is it Abhidhamma?" The word "tattha" in that question refers to the statement "I shall clarify the meaning of the Abhidhamma." It means: "In what sense is that Abhidhamma, whose meaning I promised to clarify, called Abhidhamma?" Or it means: "In what sense is the Abhidhamma mentioned in this phrase 'Abhidhammakathā' called Abhidhamma?" It is called Abhidhamma in the sense of exceeding Dhamma (dhammātireka) and distinguished Dhamma (dhammavisesa). Here, "exceeding Dhamma" means the Pali text that is superior to the Suttanta. "Distinguished Dhamma" means an extraordinary Dhamma, meaning the varied and detailed Pali text. Since "exceeding Dhamma" and "distinguished Dhamma" are themselves the meanings, it is called "dhammātireka-dhammavisesaṭṭha." Because both meanings are common as the meaning of the word "Abhidhamma," it is generally indicated in the singular. Just as in the words "abhikkamanti" and "abhikkantavaṇṇā," the prefix "abhi" indicates the sense of exceeding and distinction; therefore, it should be understood that this Dhamma is also called "Abhidhamma" because of its exceeding and distinguished meaning.

In this word "Abhidhamma," an objection might be raised: In the cases of "abhikkamanti" and "abhikkantavaṇṇā," the prefix "abhi" used before the root (kamu) is an upasagga (prefix), and thus it is appropriate that it indicates the exceeding and distinguished nature of an action (kiriya). However, the word "dhamma" is not a root; therefore, it is not even proper to use the prefix "abhi" before it. Even if it were used, prefixes only qualify actions, and since "dhamma" is not an action, it might be argued that indicating the exceeding and distinguished nature of "dhamma" is inappropriate. Such an objection is not improper (i.e., it is a valid point to raise). This is because other prefixes also...
13:
Since another prefix is seen used before a non-verbal word, indicating an excessive or special quality even for a non-action [substance], he said "Yathā" etc. to clarify this meaning by showing examples such as "atichatta" (extraordinary umbrella).

"Evameva" means: Just as the prefix "ati" used before a non-verbal word indicates that excessive or special meaning in a non-action [substance], resulting in examples like "atichatta" (extraordinary umbrella) or "visesachatta" (special umbrella), so too this Dhamma is called "Abhidhamma" because of its sense of being excessive and special compared to the [regular] Dhamma. This is because the prefix "abhi", though used before a non-verbal word, indicates that excessive or special state in a non-action Pali substance.

"Analyzed only partially" (ekadeseneva vibhattā) means: "What, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates? The form aggregate... the consciousness aggregate. And what, bhikkhus, is the form aggregate? Whatever form is past... or near, this is called the form aggregate." In this manner, they are analyzed only by way of brief exposition (uddesa) and description (niddesa). Because the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya (Abhidhamma analysis) and the Pañhapucchaka (question section), which provide further detailed explanation in the manner of "Therein, what is past form?", are absent, they are not analyzed without remainder. However, upon reaching the Abhidhamma... they are analyzed only without remainder. Therefore, this Dhamma is also called "Abhidhamma" due to its sense of being excessive and special compared to the Dhamma. This means it is due to the state of being an excessive and special Pali text of the three methods that are without remainder.

In the Suttanta, because the twenty-two faculties (indriya) do not appear together, there is no Suttanta-bhājanīya in the Indriya-vibhaṅga. In the Paṭiccasamuppāda, the causal state of various conditional phenomena (paccaya-dhamma) toward their conditionally arisen phenomena (paccayuppanna-dhamma) is briefly expounded in the manner of "With ignorance as condition, formations arise." The state of these briefly expounded phenomena as wholesome, etc., should be answered after questioning. However, since there is no formal exposition (uddesa) here stated as "Ignorance, formations," there is no question section (pañhapucchaka).

In the Suttanta, the five precepts (sikkhāpada) are briefly expounded as "abstaining from taking life," etc. If that abstinence (veramaṇī) were analyzed by way of its nature, function, etc., as "aversion, abstinence" (ārati, virati), etc., it would be the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya alone. Even if it were analyzed by way of the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda), it would still be the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya. There is no other way of analyzing abstinences by which it could be called Suttanta-bhājanīya. Therefore, there is no Suttanta-bhājanīya in the Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga.

After the Abhidhamma is known by way of word-meaning (vacanattha), he said "Pakarana-paricchedato" etc. to make it known by way of its divisions. "Only a few question cycles (pañhavāra) remain" means those that do not appear in the Dhammahadaya-vibhaṅga but appear in the Mahādhammahadaya...
14:
By the power of the words of the Dhammahadaya-vibhaṅga, the remaining question cycles (pañhavāra) are only a few. Because they are included right here in this Dhammahadaya-vibhaṅga, it is said "there is nothing new." Those remaining Pali texts are very few. If the Mahādhātukathā, which is the detailed discourse on the elements like earth, etc., is included in the Rūpakaṇḍa and Dhātuvibhaṅga, etc., or if the Mahādhātukathā, which is the detailed discourse of the Dhātukathā, does not appear in the Dhātukathā but appears only in the Mahādhātukathā, then that Pali text is very few.

To refute the statement "Discard that word because it was spoken by disciples" by showing it is the Buddha's word, he said "Sammāsambuddho hi" etc. Among the four questions: after taking the admission "Is it perceived or not perceived [by the intellect]?", the two pentads (pañcaka) that proceed by depending on and referring to the "real and ultimate sense" (sacchikaṭṭha) stated as "He who is of the real and ultimate sense" constitute one question. The one proceeding by referring to the whole body or region stated as "everywhere" (sabbattha) is one. The one proceeding by referring to time stated as "always" (sabbadā) is one. In saying "in all" (sabbesu), if the aggregates, bases, etc., are taken, the one proceeding by referring to them is one. Alternatively, there is no real and ultimate sense, region, or time that is not taken by these terms "He who is of the real and ultimate sense, everywhere, always." However, those have been investigated by taking them generally, not by way of division. Therefore, to investigate by taking them by way of division, the one proceeding by referring to the parts of the real and ultimate sense, region, and time stated as "in all" is one. Thus it is among these four questions.

Among the two pentads, here: the statement "The person is perceived... false" is one; "The person is not perceived... false" is one; "But if you think... this is your falsehood" is one; "If this is poorly refuted... this is your falsehood" is one; "It should not be refuted thus; therefore, that which you refute... is a well-performed practice" is one. Thus, performing the refutation (niggaha), performing the counter-rejoinder (paṭikamma), the wrapping of the counter-rejoinder (paṭikamma-veṭhana) by establishing the admission because of wishing for one's refutation to be a good refutation, the unraveling of the refutation (niggaha-nibbeṭhana) by showing the state of the refutation being difficult to refute through demonstrating the state of the counter-rejoinder being difficult to counter, and the cutting off by attributing the state of non-refutation, etc.—this is one pentad. In the Commentary, this is called the "Anuloma-paccanīka-pañcaka" (Direct-Reverse Pentad) in the section where the Proponent (sakavādī) leads, under the names Anuloma-pañcaka, Paṭikamma-catukka, Niggaha-catukka, Upanayana-catukka, and Nigamana-catukka. In the section where the Opponent (paravādī) leads, it is likewise called the "Paccanīkānuloma-pañcaka" (Reverse-Direct Pentad). Thus the two pentads should be known. In this same way, in the remaining questions, the eight pentads are called the "Eight-faced Logic of Debate" (aṭṭhamukhā vādayuttī).
15:
It is called *Vādayutti*. *Yutti* means the method or means; the method of a thesis (*vāda*) is *vādayutti*. It means the method for the proceeding of a thesis.

Having shown the initial refutation (*niggaha*) in the *Anuloma-paccanīka-pañcaka* (Fivefold Direct-and-Reverse), and having also shown only the initial refutation in the *Paccanīya-anuloma-pañcaka* (Fivefold Reverse-and-Direct), he said "Sā panesā" and so forth to clarify the table of contents (*mātikā*). 'Person' (*puggala*) means the self (*atta*), a being (*satta*), or a life-principle (*jīva*). '*Upalabbhati*' (is perceived) asks whether it is obtained (known) by approaching with wisdom. '*Saccikaṭṭhaparamaṭṭhena*' (in the sense of a real and ultimate fact) means asking whether it is obtained not in an unreal manner like a magic trick or a mirage, nor in the sense of something non-ultimate to be accepted through hearsay (*anussava*), but indeed in the sense of a real and ultimate fact. The other party (*paravādī*) admits it, desiring such a meaning. Again, he cross-examines with "Yo saccikaṭṭho...pe... paramaṭṭhena," asking: "If a person is obtained in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, is that person something different from those real and ultimate facts (form, feeling, etc.) and based upon them, or is he distinct from them, or is he the basis of them, or is he obtained as non-different from the nature of being affected (*ruppana*) or the nature of having causes (*sappaccaya*)?" The other party, not desiring either the difference or the non-difference of the person from form and so forth, rejects it saying, "Na hevaṃ" (Not so). Then the *Sakavādī*, considering that the other party rejects what should not be rejected because it is identical to what was already admitted, and wishing to charge him with a ground for refutation, says, "Ājānāhi niggahaṃ" (Acknowledge the refutation). When asked, "Is the person not obtained?" the *Sakavādī*, wishing to deny the view of a person (*puggala-diṭṭhi*), admits it saying, "Āmantā" (Yes). Again, the other party (*paravādī*) cross-examines with "Yo saccikaṭṭho...pe... paramaṭṭhena," asking: "If a person is not obtained in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, is he not obtained as either different or non-different from the real and ultimate fact?" because there is no other category. Since the person is not obtained in any way at all, and since for the *Sakavādī* who denies the belief in a person, the questioning about the difference or non-difference of that person is not applicable, he rejects it saying, "Na hevaṃ." The other party, seeing only a slight pretext for a consequence based on the admission and not penetrating the unerring meaning, charges him with a ground for refutation, saying, "Ājānāhi niggahaṃ."

"Iti" means because it has been shown in this way, having seen the reason for which the table of contents (*mātikā*) was established. "Yathā kinti" means in what manner does it become what is called the "Word of the Buddha" (*Buddhabhāsita*); what is the illustration of that? "Yatonidānaṃ" means because of which cause, namely the cause such as the six internal and external sense-bases (*āyatana*). "Papañcasaññāsaṅkhā" refers to the groups of perceptions associated with the obsessions (*papañca*) of craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*). "Samudācaranti" means they beset or overwhelm. In this context, among those sense-bases and so forth, there is nothing that should be delighted in, asserted, or clung to through craving, conceit, and views.
16:
Why is it said, "If it were not"? In truth, it does not exist. However, for worldlings (puthujjanas) who have not yet abandoned delighting (abhinandana), welcoming (abhivadana), and clinging (ajjhosāna), the sense bases (āyatanas) such as those to be delighted in do exist. Therefore, for those worldlings, it cannot be said "they do not exist." But for Arahants who have abandoned delighting and so forth, they do not exist in any way. Thus, it is said, "If it were not."

"This is the end" means the Path (Magga) that causes the non-existence of delighting and so forth, or the Fruit (Phala) which is the subsiding of those states, is the end or the non-occurrence of the underlying tendency to lust (rāgānusaya) and so forth.

"Knowing, he knows" means he knows all that should be known through his omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). One with only partial knowledge cannot know all that should be known. "Seeing, he sees" means he sees all that should be seen with the five eyes, namely: the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu), the Dhamma-eye (dhamma-cakkhu), the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakkhu), and the all-seeing eye (samanta-cakkhu).

Alternatively, "Knowing, he knows" means that while others who have perversions (vipallāsa), such as those who profess full understanding of the sense sphere and the fine-material sphere, may know, they know through the power of perversion. The Blessed One is not like that; having abandoned perversions, when he knows, he truly knows. Since there is no wrong view, when he sees, he truly sees.

"Become eye" (cakkhubhūta) means he is like the eye of the world because he is made of the eye of wisdom and because he causes that eye of wisdom to arise in beings. In the term "become knowledge" (ñāṇabhūta), the meaning should be understood in the same way. "Dhammas" refers to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhammas). "Brahmā" refers to the Path (Magga). He is the essence of those teachings because he arose through them and because he causes them to arise in the world.

"Speaker" (vattā) means he expounds the Four Noble Truths. "Proclaimer" (pavattā) means he speaks while causing the long-lasting penetration of the Truths. "Shower of the meaning" (atthassa ninnetā) means one who extracts and shows the meaning, or one who leads to the ultimate reality, Nibbāna. "Giver of the deathless" (amatassa dātā) means he gives the deathless by causing beings to realize the deathless Nibbāna. He is called the "Lord of Dhamma" (dhammassāmī) because the factors of enlightenment are dependent on him.

"Suvaṇṇālinga" refers to a small drum made of gold. "Su-pupphita-satapatta-sassirika" means having splendor like a well-blossomed hundred-petaled lotus.

By the words "From the time of approval... it is called the Word of the Buddha (buddhabhāsita)," it seems to imply that the act of approval is the cause for it being the Word of the Buddha. If that were so, the Kathāvatthu would not be the Word of the Buddha because it was not approved [by the Buddha himself in person]. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: Seeing that "Mahākaccāyana will analyze it in this way," the Blessed One laid down the matrix (mātikā) and entered the monastery. Accordingly, the Elder Mahākaccāyana analyzed it using the matrix laid down according to the method given by the Blessed One; thus it became the Word of the Buddha. That status as the Word of the Buddha became evident through the approval; with this intention, it is said, "Thus the Teacher... is so called."

Now, to show the arrangement of the Pali text, he says "In that Dhammasaṅgaṇī," and so forth. "From the wholesome of the sense sphere, eight" means taking the four aggregates occurring in the wholesome of the sense sphere and extracting the eight types of consciousness from them. Some also call this the "first division" (paṭhamā vibhatti). "Eighty-nine types of consciousness" refers to the Pali passages where these consciousnesses are analyzed; those Pali passages are called "eighty-nine types of consciousness." The collection of those Pali passages is called the Analysis of Consciousness (Cittavibhatti). Therefore, the statement "Eighty-nine types of consciousness... analysis" is appropriate.
17:
Now, to show the arrangement of the Pali text, he says "In that Dhammasaṅgaṇī," and so forth. "From the wholesome of the sense sphere, eight" means taking the four aggregates (with wisdom) in the wholesome of the sense sphere and extracting the eight types of consciousness from them. It is also called the ablative sense of the first division (paṭhamā vibhatti). "Eighty-nine types of consciousness" refers to the Pali passages where these consciousnesses are analyzed; those Pali passages are called "eighty-nine types of consciousness." The collection of those Pali passages is called the Analysis of Consciousness (Cittavibhatti); therefore, the statement "Eighty-nine types of consciousness is the Analysis of Consciousness" is appropriate. Since the consciousnesses are analyzed by pointing out the matrix (mātikā) and extracting each term from that matrix, the matrix is also included within the Analysis of Consciousness. Therefore, the statement "The section on the arising of consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa) is twofold by way of the matrix and the analysis of terms" is also logical.

"By way of roots" (mūlato) means the brief exposition of wholesome states and so forth by way of roots, as in "Three wholesome roots," and so forth. (He also teaches briefly) by way of aggregates as in "The aggregate of feeling," by way of doors as in "Bodily action," and by way of planes as in "In the sense sphere, the plane of happiness."

"Attha" refers to the result of a cause. "Dhamma" refers to the cause. The inclusion by way of cause, as in "Three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots," is the summary (nikkhepa) by way of Dhamma. The inclusion by way of cause and result, as in "Associated with that, the defilements arising from that and sharing the same basis," is the summary by way of Attha.

Alternatively, "Dhamma" refers to the Pali text as spoken, and "Attha" refers to the meaning of the spoken Pali text. "Three wholesome causes" is Dhamma (Pali). "Therein, what are the three wholesome causes? Non-greed..." and so forth is Attha (meaning), and it is also called Dhamma (Pali) again. "Therein, what is non-greed?" and so forth is Attha. In this way, the summary should be understood by way of Attha and Dhamma.

"By way of name" (nāmato) means (summarizing) the states taught as "Three wholesome roots" by way of names such as non-greed and so forth. "By way of gender" (lingato) means summarizing the very same single state pointed out by way of genders such as the masculine, as in "Non-greed (alobho), the act of not being greedy (alubhanā), the state of not being greedy (alubhitattaṃ)."

"The course of counting" (gaṇanacāraṃ) refers to the process of counting. "They equalize" (samānenti) means they make equal or they fulfill; it is the same in the case of "should be equalized" (samānetabbaṃ). Regarding states already known in this Abhidhamma, such as "Those sharing in knowledge, those sharing in ignorance," when the Abhidhamma-specialist elders listen to or contemplate the Suttas, they do not become weary when terms like "those sharing in knowledge" appear in the Suttas because the meaning is already known. With this intention, it is said, "It is established so that the Abhidhamma-specialist elders... do not become weary."
18:
Anamatagga means having an unknown beginning or limit. Khandhantara refers to the distinction between the aggregates or the body itself. The subtle Dhamma is called Saṇhasukhumadhamma (subtle and delicate Dhamma) because it cannot be grasped by ordinary knowledge and must be grasped only by subtle and refined wisdom. It is called Balava (powerful) because it arises with a strong momentum of knowledge and because it is the cause of that strong momentum of knowledge. Gambhīragata refers to that which has a profound nature, or it is called Gambhīragata because there are profound occurrences within that Dhamma. Yathānupubbaṃ means in due order. Nikhilena means taught without remainder, or taught by the Blessed One who is free from the five mental shackles (khila). Rūpagataṃ vā is like seeing a gem in one's hand with the eye. "He who sees the Samantapaṭṭhāna (Universal Conditional Relations) with penetrative knowledge, he indeed exists, not that he does not exist," said the Elder Mahākassapa, referring to himself.

Among the eight hundred and one defilements mentioned in the Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga, if one removes the one hundred and eight ways of craving (taṇhā-vicarita) and combines the remaining six hundred and ninety-three defilements with the sixty-two types of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), and multiplies them by two (as arisen and unarisen), there are one thousand five hundred and ten defilements. Since a slight deficiency or excess is not counted, they are called the "one thousand five hundred defilements." It should be understood that the remaining ways of craving are not taken into account in the exhaustion of defilements because they are not considered in terms of the past, etc.

Mecakapaṭā refers to dark blue or black cloths. In the phrase "cittasamuṭṭhānā vaṇṇadhātu," the meaning should be taken as the color-element arising from the temperature (utu) which has the mind as its root cause. Why? Because matter born of the mind does not go outside the body. However, it is said so because it arises in a sequence of matter born of the mind. Alternatively, in this phrase "cittasamuṭṭhānā vaṇṇadhātu," the words "paccaya" (condition) and "utu" (temperature) are omitted, and the same meaning as mentioned before should be taken. This is like the beauty of complexion (suvaṇṇatā) and the goodness of voice (sussaratā). Here, although "sussaratā" is mentioned in the context of kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa), the sound itself is not kamma-born matter. Therefore, it is said so because it depends on the lips, palate, etc., which are kamma-born matter. Similarly, here too, "cittasamuṭṭhānā vaṇṇadhātu" is said referring to what arises from the temperature which has the mind as its root cause.

Kāyasakkhi means personal witness (direct experience). Dantāvaraṇa refers to the pair of lips. Mukhādāna refers to the mouth opening. Siliṭṭha means being well-connected and well-situated. Sare nimittaṃ gahetvā means taking the sign by the power of the sound of Dhamma, thinking "this sound is the Dhamma," and not by the power of signs that cause defilements. In the phrase "ekappahārena," pahāra refers to one-third of a day (one watch). Evaṃ sante means that without taking the previously mentioned words, one takes only the statement that the sequence of the Pali text originated from the Elder, and by that statement, one refutes the previous words and raises an objection.
19:
The phrase "tene-tam-etassa" refers to the meaning of the Vinaya. "The varieties such as one's own benefit, others' benefit, etc." means that if a person recites, hears, teaches, contemplates, or preaches that Sutta, the benefits such as virtue (sīla) contained in that Sutta belong to that person. Since that person can also accomplish benefits for others, it also belongs to others. That Sutta indicates and clarifies both types of benefits. Similarly, benefits of the present life, benefits of the future life, mundane benefits, supramundane benefits, and so on, are included by the word "ādi" (etc.). Here, the word "attha" is a synonymous term meaning benefit (hita); it does not mean the literal meaning of the spoken words (bhāsitattha).

If one were to take only the literal meaning of the spoken words, it would mean that a Sutta indicates its own spoken meaning and also the meaning of another Sutta. In reality, since the meaning clearly shown by one Sutta is only the meaning of that Sutta, it is impossible for that Sutta to show the meaning of another Sutta. Therefore, since there is no meaning of another Sutta to be excluded, it is not necessary to use the word "atta" (self/own). Since there is no spoken meaning that is separate from one's own benefit and others' benefit, it is also not necessary to use the word "ādi" (etc.). Therefore, because the aforementioned benefits cannot exist directly in the Sutta, they are spoken of as one's own benefit and others' benefit by virtue of the person who upholds the Sutta.

Alternatively, without considering the Sutta itself, it means that the Sutta indicates the varieties of benefits mentioned in the Niddesa: own benefit (attattha), others' benefit (parattha), benefit of both (ubhayattha), benefit of the present life (diṭṭhadhammika-attha), benefit of the future life (samparāyika-attha), evident meaning (uttāna-attha), profound meaning (gambhīra-attha), hidden meaning (guḷha-attha), concealed meaning (paṭicchanna-attha), meaning to be inferred (neyya-attha), direct meaning (nīta-attha), blameless benefit (anavajja-attha), benefit free from defilements (nikkilesa-attha), pure benefit (vodāna-attha), and ultimate benefit (paramattha-attha).

Or else, it indicates one's own benefit as in "he himself is one of few desires," and others' benefit as in "he is one who speaks to others about having few desires." In this way, Suttas such as "he himself is one who abstains from taking life," etc., should be applied. The meaning of the word "Sutta" should be stated so as to distinguish it from the Vinaya and Abhidhamma. Therefore, in the teaching (desanā) that proceeds by the power of the inclination (ajjhāsaya) of those to be tamed (veneyya), one's own benefit, others' benefit, etc., are shown very clearly. It is not so in the teaching (Vinaya and Abhidhamma) that proceeds by the power of authority (āṇā) and the nature of Dhamma (dhamma-sabhāva). Because it indicates such benefits, it is called "Sutta."

In the Sutta, authority and the nature of Dhamma follow the inclination of those to be tamed. Unlike in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, where the inclination of those to be tamed must follow authority and the nature of Dhamma, in the Sutta, the inclination of those to be tamed does not have to follow authority and the nature of Dhamma. Therefore, because it is a Suttanta teaching that leads to the absolute benefit of those to be tamed, it is said, "In this Sutta, the benefits are well-spoken," and so on. "Pasavatī" means it yields results (bears fruit). To clarify the meaning of the phrase "atthānaṃ sūcanato," the word "sūcayati" is used.
20:
(The Sutta) produces benefits. To clarify the meaning of the expression 'Suttāṇā,' it is said: 'It protects beings well.' One should apply the authoritative nature of the Sutta and its capacity to encompass those benefits in the arrangement of one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth. Since the Sutta is primary in revealing those benefits, its distinction from the other [Pitakas], the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, should also be applied. 'Etaṃ' refers to the verse that explains the meaning, beginning with 'Atthānaṃ sūcanato.' 'Etassa' refers to the meaning of the word 'Sutta.'

In the word 'Abhikkamanti,' the prefix 'Abhi-' indicates the increase or excellence of the action of going (kamana). In the word 'Abhikkantena,' it also shows the excellence or distinction of the action of pleasing (kanti). This is appropriate because a prefix (upasagga) qualifies the verb. In words like 'Abhiññātā,' 'Abhirājā,' and 'Abhivinaye,' the prefix 'Abhi-' occurs in contexts such as night, etc., which are marked, honored, or delimited. If one asks how these are appropriate: they are appropriate because they indicate actions such as marking, knowing, honoring, and delimiting, and because night, the king, and the Vinaya are associated with those actions. They are increased by the development of meditation (bhāvanā-vuddhi) and by pervasion (pharaṇa-vuddhi). 'Ārammaṇādīhi' means by way of object (ārammaṇa), association (sampayutta), kamma, door (dvāra), practice (paṭipadā), and so forth. 'Avisitthaṃ' refers to the word 'Piṭaka,' which is common and not distinct among the mutually distinct Vinaya, Suttanta, and Abhidhamma. 'Yathāvutteneiva' means by the method beginning with 'in this way, by the two kinds of meaning.'

The giving and making known of the meanings to be taught through the arrangement of authority (āṇā), etc., pertaining to the teacher, is called 'Desanā' (Teaching). Instruction, training, and teaching (Sāsana) is the act of disciplining according to the fault, etc., residing in the person to be taught. 'Kathā' (Discourse) is the speaking of the meanings to be taught, such as restraint (saṃvara) and non-restraint (asaṃvara), and the making of connections with speech. The word 'bheda' (distinction/variety) should be applied respectively as: 'One should properly illustrate the variety of teaching (desanā-bheda), the variety of instruction (sāsana-bheda), and the variety of discourse (kathā-bheda).' 'Bheda' means distinction or differentiation. One should also illustrate the three trainings (sikkhā), the three abandonments (pahāna), and the state of profundity. 'Yaṃ' refers to the scriptures (pariyatti), etc. 'Yathā' means by various ways such as learning (pariyāpuṇana) due to reasons like refutation (upārambha), etc.

In the statement that these four—Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha—exist in these three Pitakas, the meaning of the text (tanti-attha), the teaching of the text (tanti-desanā), and the penetration of the meaning of the text (tanti-attha-paṭivedha) are the domains of the text. Therefore, it is appropriate that the Vinaya Pitaka, etc., are the foundations for Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha. However, since the Pitakas are themselves the texts (tanti), how is it appropriate for them to be the foundation of Dhamma (the text)? (If one objects thus:) It is appropriate because the collection of texts is the foundation for the individual parts of the text. Because Dhamma, etc., are difficult to plunge into, the Vinaya, etc., are said to be profound due to those [four]: Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha. Thus, the four kinds of profundity of the Vinaya, etc., are stated. Therefore, 'Only Dhamma, etc., are profound because they are difficult to plunge into...'
21:
## It should not be objected: 'Are the Vinaya and other Pitakas not profound?'

It should not be objected that 'the Vinaya and other Pitakas are not profound.' Among those four (Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, Paṭivedha), because penetration (paṭivedha) is difficult to achieve, the difficulty of plunging into Dhamma and Attha should be understood; and because the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) is difficult to achieve, the difficulty of plunging into Desanā should be understood. As for penetration (paṭivedha), its difficulty of plunging should be understood because it is impossible [for ordinary people] to produce, and because the arising of knowledge that takes that penetration as its object is difficult.

If it is asked: 'How is the state of Dhamma as a cause known through this definition: "Knowledge of the cause is Dhammapaṭisambhidā" (hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā)?' It is because the Buddha, in showing the meaning of the component words of the compound 'Dhammapaṭisambhidā,' taught 'hetumhi ñāṇaṃ' (knowledge of the cause). Indeed, in this text 'dhamme paṭisambhidā,' the Buddha, in showing the meaning of the word 'dhamme,' taught 'hetumhi' (in the cause); and in showing the meaning of the word 'paṭisambhidā,' he taught 'ñāṇaṃ' (knowledge). Therefore, the Buddha established the state of Dhamma as a cause by showing this meaning: that the words 'hetu' and 'dhamma' have the same meaning, and the words 'ñāṇa' and 'paṭisambhidā' also have the same meaning. The state of Attha as cause and effect (phala) should be understood in the same way.

In the text 'yathādhammaṃ,' the word 'dhamma' includes everything—both the cause and the effect of the cause. That word 'dhamma' is a term expressing nature (sabhāva); it does not express the meaning of cause as scripture (pariyatti). Therefore, 'yathādhammaṃ' means: whatever Dhamma there is, such as ignorance (avijjā) and formations (saṅkhāra), in that specific Dhamma. 'Dhammābhilāpa' is the correct, non-perverted expression (abhilāpa) that makes the meaning clear. By this term 'dhammābhilāpa,' the Buddha shows the 'Dhamma-nirutti' (linguistic expression of Dhamma) taught in the Vibhaṅga Pali: 'Among those [paṭisambhidās], the knowledge of the expression of words uttered to reveal the Dhamma is Niruttipaṭisambhidā.' By the phrase 'teaching by way of accordance (anuloma), etc.,' he shows the expression of that Dhamma-nirutti, the teaching, and the utterance of that speech. By the word 'adhippāya' (intention), he shows that the statement 'Teaching is a designation (paññatti)' was said with reference to the ultimate term (paramattha-sadda) which is Dhamma-nirutti, and not with reference to a designation (paññatti) that is divorced from that ultimate term.

'That realization (abhisamaya) is mundane and supramundane.' To make clear the manner in which one realizes the realization thus described, what one realizes, and what its nature is, he said: 'It is the understanding of Dhamma, etc., in accordance with the benefit (attha), etc., by way of object and by way of non-delusion.' Among those, understanding Dhamma, etc., in accordance with the benefit, etc., by way of object, is mundane realization, which has as its object the designation of the cause such as ignorance, the effect such as formations, and both. Understanding Dhamma, etc., in accordance with the benefit, etc., by way of non-delusion, is supramundane realization, which has Nibbāna as its object, is associated with the Path, and destroys delusion regarding the aforementioned Dhamma, Attha, and Paññatti. To show another meaning of penetration (paṭivedha) besides realization (abhisamaya), he said: 'Or of those various (forms, etc.)...'
22:
By the etymological definition, “Penetration is *paṭivedha*,” it refers to *abhisamaya* (attainment/realization). By the definition, “That which is penetrated is *paṭivedha*,” it is also appropriate to call the unperverted nature (true nature) of various phenomena such as materiality (*rūpa*) and so on, *paṭivedha*.

In order to show the profound nature of the Piṭakas through the aforementioned *dhamma* and so on, it is said: “Now, because in these Piṭakas,” and so forth. It should be understood by connecting thus: whatever penetration there is in the various *dhamma* contained within these respective Piṭakas, and whatever unperverted nature of those various *dhamma* there is in these Piṭakas. The difficulty of penetration (*dukkho-gāhatā*) should also be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The distinction here is that *paṭivedha*, known as the unperverted nature, is difficult to penetrate (*dukkho-gāha*) solely because it is difficult to understand.

The word “*yaṃ*” is spoken with reference to the improper learning of the *pariyatti* (scriptures). “*Attha*” refers to the meaning of the spoken Pali text and the meaning of its purpose (benefit). “*Na upaparikkhandi*” means they do not investigate. “*Na nijjhānaṃ khamanti*” means they cannot endure (attain) the wisdom of thorough reflection; the meaning is that they are unable to take up the teaching by seeing it with wisdom and delighting in it after thorough reflection. “*Iti*” means that in this way, they learn the Dhamma for the sake of the benefit of being released from the arguments (*vādappamokkha*) that others have placed upon them. “*Vādappamokkha*” means release from blame. It means they learn the Dhamma moderately for the sake of fulfilling virtue (*sīla*) and so on, or for the sake of liberation without clinging (*anupādā-vimokkha*). They do not experience (do not obtain) the essence of that Dhamma. For them, because those teachings were improperly learned, they lead to harm and suffering for a long time due to causes such as disparaging others, conceit, arrogance, and malice (*palāsa*). One appointed to a storehouse is called a storekeeper (*bhaṇḍāgārika*). Because he is like a storekeeper, he is called a storekeeper (*bhaṇḍāgārika*), a guardian of the Dhamma-treasure. The *pariyatti* of an Arahant who, like a storekeeper, guards it without expecting any other benefit, is called *bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti*.

The restriction with the word *eva* in “*tāsaṃyeva*” is spoken with reference to the fact that the six supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) that are to be attained are not taught in detail in the Vinaya Piṭaka. This is because in the *Verañja-kaṇḍa*, only the three knowledges (*vijjā*) are analyzed in detail. The restriction in the second “*tāsaṃyeva*” is made with regard to the four analytical insights, not the three knowledges. This is because those three knowledges are included within the six supernormal powers and have already been analyzed in the Sutta Piṭaka. It should be connected as “having known and collected.” It refers to the entirety of the Buddha’s word in the various Piṭakas.

It is called *anulomika* (conformable) because its name is in accordance with its meaning. To clarify this conformable nature, it is said: “But why,” and so forth. “Even a single collection” (*eka-nikāya*) is also meant.
23:
King Poṇika and King Cikkhallika were of the warrior caste (*khattiya*); their dwellings were called *Poṇika-nikāya* and *Cikkhallika-nikāya*. Similarly, after defining the Buddha’s word and the Piṭakas as the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates (*dhammakkhandha*), the passage beginning with “*evametaṃ sabbampi*” was started to show that all the divisions, such as the First Buddha-word, and other divisions like the summaries (*uddāna-saṅgaha*), are known through the Council (*Saṅgīti*), which was adorned by the manifestation of many wonders. By designating this Abhidhamma as the *Abhidhamma Piṭaka* among the Piṭakas, it should be understood that its status as the Middle Buddha-word (*majjhima-buddhāvacana*) is shown, as well as the fact that the Tathāgata was an *Abhidhammika* (expert in Abhidhamma) from the very beginning.

Here, it might be said: “If the fact that the Abhidhamma was spoken by the Tathāgata were established, its status as the Middle Buddha-word would also be established; but that very fact is not yet established.” To prove that the Abhidhamma was spoken by the Buddha (*Buddha-bhāsita*) using the Vinaya and other sources, the teacher said: “While the monks were memorizing it,” and so forth. “The assembly of all occasions” (*sabba-sāmayika-parisā*) refers to the assembly that learns all five Nikāyas. It is said “not learned” because the entire Vinaya Piṭaka had not yet been learned. It is said “learned only the Vinaya” because the two *Vibhaṅgas* (Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga and Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga) had been learned. The Blessed One demonstrated that the Abhidhamma was spoken by the Buddha by declaring that there is no offense for a monk who, without wishing to disparage the Vinaya, says “Learn the Abhidhamma,” and by declaring a *pācittiya* offense for a nun who asks a question to a monk who has not been given permission regarding the Abhidhamma. This is because the Abhidhamma is taught together with the Suttas and other teachings spoken by the Buddha, and because such statements are absent in external (non-Buddhist) scriptures.

Even stronger than this is the fact that the Buddha cut off doubt by giving praise to an *Abhidhammika*. One who confuses the distinction between kammas (*kammantara*), such as describing a sense-sphere kamma as a fine-material sphere kamma, or a kamma with dark results as a kamma with white results, is one who stirs up and destroys the Dhamma.

“*Jina-cakka*” refers to the Dispensation (*Sāsana*) of the Conqueror. “*Visaṃvādeti*” means to deceive or to lead astray. Among the grounds for schism, it is clearly seen in one instance as: “Showing what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as not spoken and not uttered, and what was not spoken and not uttered as spoken and uttered.” The same should be said hereafter. To make clear the obscure time, place, teacher, and audience, there should be a prologue (*nidāna*) accompanied by those instructions. However, since it is not the domain of others, the Teacher (the Buddha) is already well-known; the time is also well-known because the time of his descent into the womb and so on is clear; and the place and audience are well-known because of the fact that it was taught in the celestial realm. Therefore, what need would there be for the function of a prologue?
24:
That teaching in which the aggregates and so forth are analyzed exhaustively (without remainder) is called Abhidhamma. Therefore, with the intention that the origin of that Abhidhamma should also be in the place where the aggregates and so forth were penetrated without remainder, the Elder Tissabhūti showed: "The Abhidhamma has the Great Enlightenment as its origin" (Mahābodhinidāno Abhidhammo). By the method beginning with "I know thus; feeling is experienced also because of right view," he dwelt by means of the aggregate of feeling and so forth, which are parts of the aggregates, while investigating feeling through causes and so forth. "Dhamme" refers to the states (dhammas) beginning with the wholesome (kusala) and ending with the Araṇa dyad.

"Dhammāṃ parivattento" means that while reciting and rehearsing the Pāḷi text together with the Commentary, he reached the point of challenge by this opponent and said, "This person is an opponent," and so forth. While those like me who know the origin and are a refuge are present, it is like one wailing in the forest without a refuge; and while we who are witnesses to the existence of the origin are present, it is like conducting a case without witnesses. He does not even know the existence of the origin. Speaking thus, "Is this not the origin?", he said this. "Ekameva" (only one) means there is only one origin of teaching (desanānidāna) because it was taught according to the inclinations of those to be led (veneyya). "Dve nidānāni" (two origins) means there are two kinds of origins because it was taught according to the Dhamma to be realized and the Dhamma to be taught. The basis of the Omniscient Knowledge, which is the cause for penetrating the Abhidhamma, is called "Adhigamanidāna" (origin of realization) because it is as if it bestows the realization. With which faith he directed his mind toward the knowledge of the path of Arahatship and the Omniscient Knowledge in the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, and made the aspiration.

## Explanation of the Story of Sumedha
"Caturo ca asaṅkhiye" (four incalculables) means that by ascending and counting back through past time, it should be understood by connecting the remaining words that there was once a city named "Amara". "Dasahi" (with ten) means [it was not devoid of] the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, drums, conch shells, kettledrums, lutes, singing, and cymbals, as well as the tenth sound: "Eat, drink, and consume!" To show these ten kinds of sounds partially, he said "hatthisaddaṃ" (the sound of elephants) and so forth. In the word "hatthisaddaṃ", the accusative case should be seen in the sense of the instrumental. It should be construed as "not devoid of the sounds of drums, conch shells, and chariots" or as "resounded with". Alternatively, "hatthisaddaṃ" refers to the city that has the sound of elephants. In the passage "khādatha pivatha ceva", it should be understood that the word "iti" is not explicitly used because its meaning is already understood.

It was endowed with all the features of a city because it was complete with gardens, lotus ponds, and so forth. "Lakkhaṇe" refers to the treatises on the marks of women and the marks of men; "itihāse" refers to the Purāṇas; "sadhamme" refers to his own Dhamma of the three knowledges (tevijjā) and the procedures for sacrifice and so forth; "pāramiṃ" refers to [the brahmin named Sumedha] who has reached the perfection of knowledge that goes to the further shore. "Cintesahaṃ" means "I, being Sumedha, reflected," thus the Blessed One said.
25:
